clinicalPearls: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is the cause of heterophile-positive infectious mononucleosis (IM), classically marked by the triad of fever, sore throat (pharyngitis), and lymphadenopathy, together with atypical lymphocytosis (Harrison 22e p.1508).

EBV is spread mainly by contact with oral secretions (saliva); by adulthood >90% of individuals are seropositive. IM is typically a disease of young adults, while in young children primary infection is usually asymptomatic or a mild pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509).

The incubation period in young adults is about 4-6 weeks, often preceded by a 1-2 week prodrome of fatigue, malaise, and myalgia before fever, sore throat, and lymphadenopathy appear (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Lymphadenopathy (most often posterior cervical, tender, symmetric, not fixed) and pharyngitis are most prominent in the first 2 weeks, whereas splenomegaly is more prominent during the second and third weeks (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Lymphadenopathy and fever are the most common signs (each in >90%), with pharyngitis/tonsillitis in ~82% and splenomegaly in ~51%; tonsillar exudate can resemble streptococcal pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1509).

Characteristic laboratory features: leukocytosis peaking at the second-to-third week with >10% atypical lymphocytes (enlarged cells with abundant cytoplasm, predominantly CD8+ T cells), often with mild neutropenia and thrombocytopenia (Harrison 22e p.1509).
Abnormal liver function (mildly elevated aminotransferases and alkaline phosphatase) occurs in >90% of cases, with hyperbilirubinemia in about 40% (Harrison 22e p.1509).

The heterophile (and the somewhat more sensitive Monospot) test is the standard diagnostic test in children and adults; heterophile antibodies do not interact with EBV proteins. Tests are positive in ~40% in week 1 and 80-90% by week 3, so repeat testing may be needed if performed early (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Heterophile antibodies are often absent in children under 5 years, the elderly, and patients with atypical presentations; in these cases EBV-specific serology should be used (Harrison 22e p.1511).

EBV-specific serology pattern: IgM antibody to viral capsid antigen (VCA) is most useful for acute IM (present only during the first 2-3 months); IgG anti-VCA persists for life and indicates past exposure; antibodies to EBNA appear late (3-6 weeks after symptom onset) and persist for life (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Most cases of IM are self-limited; most patients have symptoms for 2-4 weeks, but nearly 10% have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more (Harrison 22e p.1509).

EBV is associated with several malignancies, including Burkitt's lymphoma (~90% of African cases, ~15% of US cases), anaplastic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (uniformly EBV-associated in southern China), gastric carcinoma (the most common EBV-associated malignancy worldwide), Hodgkin's lymphoma (especially mixed-cellularity type), and various T-/NK-cell and CNS lymphomas; EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disease occurs in immunodeficient and transplant patients (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511).

Large epidemiologic data show a strong association of EBV with multiple sclerosis; one study of over a million military personnel found a 32-fold higher MS risk after primary EBV infection, though the causal role still requires further research (Harrison 22e p.1508, 1511).
harrison.pathophysiology: EBV, a herpesvirus, is transmitted in saliva and infects oropharyngeal and salivary epithelium plus B lymphocytes (including tonsillar-crypt lymphocytes directly), then disseminates via the bloodstream. Proliferation of EBV-infected B cells alongside reactive T cells enlarges lymphoid tissue. During acute IM up to 1 in 100 peripheral B cells is infected (falling to 1-50 per million after recovery), and there is an inverted CD4+/CD8+ ratio with large clonal CD8+ T-cell expansions (up to 40% directed against EBV antigens). The EBV receptor on B cells is CD21 (the C3d complement receptor); HLA class II is a co-receptor for B-cell entry, while epithelial entry uses ephrin A2. Memory B cells (not epithelial cells) are the lifelong reservoir. Cellular immunity (NK cells, cytotoxic T cells recognizing EBNAs and LMPs) is more important than humoral immunity in control; if T-cell immunity is impaired, infected B cells may proliferate, and in EBV-associated tumors LMP-1 mimics TNF-receptor-family signaling (e.g., CD40) to drive growth (Harrison 22e p.1508-1509).
additionalDifferentials: CMV infection (the most common cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis; older age, longer fever, exudative pharyngitis uncommon) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Acute HIV infection (diffuse rash, oral/genital ulcers, aseptic meningitis) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Toxoplasmosis (less splenomegaly; exposure to cats or raw meat) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
HHV-6 infection (older age at presentation) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Streptococcal pharyngitis (no splenomegaly, less fatigue) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Drug reaction, most often to phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, or minocycline (can occur at any age) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
nonInfectiousMimics: Lymphoma (fixed, nontender nodes; atypical lymphocytes) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Drug-induced mononucleosis-like reaction (phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, minocycline) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
additionalInvestigations: Heterophile antibody test (titer >=40 diagnostic with compatible symptoms and atypical lymphocytes), or the more sensitive commercial Monospot test (~75% sensitive, ~90% specific vs EBV-specific serology) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
EBV-specific serology: IgM and IgG anti-VCA, anti-EBNA, and (less useful for routine diagnosis) anti-early antigen (EA-D, EA-R) (Harrison 22e p.1511)
Peripheral blood examination for atypical lymphocytes and CBC (leukocytosis, possible neutropenia/thrombocytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1509)
Liver function tests (aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin) (Harrison 22e p.1509)

EBV DNA detection by PCR in blood or CSF (useful when serology is equivocal, in CNS lymphoma in AIDS, and for monitoring lymphoproliferative disease); throat or blood culture is NOT helpful because EBV persists for life in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511)
redFlags: Splenic rupture (occurs in <0.5% of cases, more common in males; may present as abdominal pain, referred shoulder pain, or hemodynamic compromise) - a leading cause of the rare deaths from IM (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Upper-airway obstruction from tonsillar/adenoidal hypertrophy or epiglottic/pharyngeal/uvular edema (Harrison 22e p.1510)

CNS complications (meningitis, encephalitis, cerebellar ataxia, cranial nerve palsies especially CN VII, Guillain-Barre syndrome, transverse myelitis) - usually within the first 2 weeks (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Coombs-positive, cold agglutinins to red-cell i antigen, ~2% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, severe cytopenias (red-cell aplasia, severe granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, pancytopenia) (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Fulminant hepatitis, myocarditis/pericarditis, pneumonia with pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.1510)
Fatal IM in patients with X-linked lymphoproliferative disease or other primary immunodeficiencies - and rarely in patients with no obvious preexisting immune defect (Harrison 22e p.1510)
harrison.prognosis: Most cases of IM are self-limited and resolve over 2-4 weeks; deaths are very rare and are most often due to CNS complications, splenic rupture, upper-airway obstruction, or bacterial superinfection. Nearly 10% of patients have fatigue persisting for 6 months or more. Disease severity correlates with blood CD8+ T-cell and EBV DNA levels. Most neurologic complications resolve without sequelae. The risk of EBV-positive Hodgkin's lymphoma is significantly increased in young adults for several years after EBV-seropositive IM (Harrison 22e p.1509-1511).
pitfalls: Ampicillin/penicillin rash pitfall: about 95% of patients with infectious mononucleosis given ampicillin develop a rash; classically a macular rash followed penicillin-derivative use, although more recent studies suggest EBV-associated rashes may occur at similar frequency with or without penicillin exposure, and these rashes are not predictive of future penicillin reactions (Harrison 22e p.1509, 1513).

Heterophile/Monospot tests are often falsely negative early in illness (positive in only ~40% during week 1) and are unreliable in children under 5, the elderly, and atypical presentations - repeat testing or EBV-specific serology may be required (Harrison 22e p.1511).
False-positive Monospot results are more common in connective tissue disease, lymphoma, viral hepatitis, and malaria (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Culture of EBV from throat washings or blood does NOT diagnose acute infection because the virus persists lifelong in the oropharynx and B cells (Harrison 22e p.1511).
Glucocorticoids are NOT indicated for uncomplicated IM and may predispose to bacterial superinfection (Harrison 22e p.1512).
Acyclovir has had no significant clinical impact on IM in controlled trials (Harrison 22e p.1512).

Persistent EBV infection is NOT a cause of chronic fatigue syndrome; antibody titers in such patients are not significantly different from healthy seropositive adults and EBV DNA is not elevated (Harrison 22e p.1510-1511).
management: Manage supportively with rest, adequate fluids and antipyretic or analgesic agents such as paracetamol or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory, as most cases are self-limiting
Avoid ampicillin and amoxicillin, which commonly precipitate a morbilliform rash
Advise avoidance of contact and collision sports until splenomegaly has resolved, to reduce the risk of splenic rupture
Reserve corticosteroids for complications such as impending airway obstruction from tonsillar enlargement, severe thrombocytopenia or haemolytic anaemia
Manage acute complications including splenic rupture, upper-airway obstruction and neurological involvement urgently
Treat bacterial superinfection such as coexisting streptococcal pharyngitis with appropriate antibiotics, avoiding aminopenicillins
Recognise that antivirals are not routinely indicated, reserving intensive management for EBV-driven lymphoproliferative disease in the immunocompromised
